awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Development of a High-Throughput Fecal Exfoliome Analyzing Platform for Clinical Drug Development
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project lies in enabling pharmaceutical companies to better evaluate and tailor treatments for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a chronic condition that affects over 3 million people in the United States. Drug development for IBD is hindered by the lack of scalable, non-invasive tools for monitoring disease activity and understanding patient variation. This project addresses that gap by developing a stool-based platform capable of capturing real-time molecular information about gut health. Unlike invasive procedures like endoscopy or conventional stool tests that offer only limited insight, this method provides a more detailed, data-rich view of gastrointestinal function over time. By helping pharmaceutical companies evaluate new drugs, identify patients most likely to benefit, and improve the design of clinical trials, this technology holds the potential to boost success rates and lower development costs. The platform is designed for integration into pharmaceutical pipelines through sustainable business models with near-term revenue and long-term licensing opportunities. On top of its commercial potential, this technology aims to advance public health by enabling more personalized treatment strategies and better outcomes for people living with IBD.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project addresses a long-standing challenge in healthcare for gut disorders: how to non-invasively access meaningful information about the human gut. Stool contains human genetic material shed from the lining of the intestine, but analyzing this material has been difficult due to the overwhelming presence of microbes and food debris. This project builds on a method that captures human gene activity from stool and aims to expand its use in drug development. The project will enhance the method to measure the activity of over 2,000 genes related to gut health and immune function, develop software tools to interpret the data, and apply the approach to biobanked stool samples from patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). By connecting gene activity patterns in stool with how patients responded to specific drug treatments, this research may help identify genetic signals that predict whether a treatment will work. The anticipated results will demonstrate how stool samples could guide more personalized and effective treatment design for people with gut disorders and support the development of new therapies.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Foli Bio is developing Foli-seq to make detailed intestinal status available from a simple stool sample that can be collected at home. Our goal is to help drug developers understand how treatments affect intestinal disease and ultimately give patients more convenient ways to monitor their health and guide treatment decisions. Foli-seq measures RNA molecules from human cells naturally shed from the intestinal lining, providing nearly 2,000 quantitative signals about inflammation, the intestinal barrier, tissue repair, and other gut functions. This approach provides molecular information about the intestinal lining without requiring a colonoscopy for each measurement. With NSF Phase I support, Foli Bio advanced the laboratory method and developed tools to interpret these signals. Repeated measurements of the same material showed high correlation and the analyses identified patterns associated with different intestinal regions.

Through scientific collaborations, we profiled more than 270 samples from patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We analyzed these results alongside existing development datasets generated using the advanced Foli-seq method. The resulting data resource brought together stool RNA measurements and clinical information about disease activity and treatment outcomes. This work produced two biomarker panels, each combining multiple RNA signals into a meaningful biological pattern. The first was associated with disease activity in the intestinal lining. We compared it with endoscopy, which uses a camera to examine the intestine, and fecal calprotectin, an established stool test for inflammation. The second identified patterns present before treatment that were associated with subsequent response to anti-TNF medicines, a commonly used treatment for IBD. These patterns included differences in repair, barrier, and immune activity, providing information about the intestinal biology associated with treatment response.

These results establish a foundation for reusable biomarkers that could make clinical studies faster and more informative. Our next step is to standardize biomarker scoring and reporting and apply these tools across additional patient groups and treatment studies. Convenient, repeated stool sampling could give researchers earlier and more detailed evidence of how a medicine affects the intestine. This information could help them identify promising treatments sooner, understand why patients respond differently, and design more effective clinical studies. Our goal is to shorten the path from promising discoveries to effective new medicines, helping more treatments reach people living with IBD. The longer-term opportunity extends to patient care. We envision accessible stool tests that help patients monitor disease between clinic visits, detect changes that warrant attention, and help clinicians select treatments based on each patient’s intestinal biology. This precision medicine approach would support more timely decisions and treatment that better fits each patient.
